lessonCatalog.title: Identify causes of disease
lessonCatalog.question: What makes a microbe a pathogen?
ideas: A disease is a condition that disrupts normal body function. Some diseases are caused by pathogens: disease-causing bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists or parasites. A microbe is not automatically harmful.
Bacteria are cells that can multiply under suitable conditions. Viruses need host cells to reproduce. Identifying the cause matters because prevention and treatment depend on it.
lessonCatalog.model: A person becomes ill after eating contaminated food. The investigation asks what organism was present, how it entered the food and which conditions allowed it to grow; symptoms alone do not identify the cause.
lessonCatalog.check: Which statement about microbes is accurate?
options: Some microbes are pathogens, while many are not
lessonCatalog.writing: Explain why identifying a pathogen and its route of spread helps plan prevention.

lessonCatalog.title: Interrupt spread and protect food
lessonCatalog.question: How do environment and handling change disease risk?
ideas: Communicable diseases can spread between hosts through routes such as air, water, food and contact. Non-communicable conditions do not spread from person to person by infection.

Food preservation changes the conditions in which microbes grow. Refrigeration slows growth, heating can kill many organisms, and drying removes needed water. Clean handling and suitable storage reduce risk.
lessonCatalog.model: For a picnic, the practical question is whether perishable food stayed at a safe temperature and avoided cross-contamination. A food item that looks normal is not proof that it is safe.
lessonCatalog.check: What is the main purpose of refrigeration for perishable food?
options: To turn food into a vaccine
lessonCatalog.writing: Plan a safer picnic: name two possible contamination routes and a matching prevention action for each.

lessonCatalog.title: Understand outbreaks in society
lessonCatalog.question: Why can the same pathogen have different effects in different communities?
ideas: An epidemic is a rise of disease in a community or region; a pandemic spreads across many countries or continents. These words describe spread, not how severe every case will be.
Crowding, travel, clean water, access to care and prior exposure affect community outcomes. Historical examples in the source textbook require attention to the people, time and conditions involved.
lessonCatalog.model: If an infection appears in two communities, compare water systems, housing, transport and available care before explaining different outcomes. A single factor seldom explains the whole pattern.
options: Geographic spread across many countries or continents
A disease caused only by bacteria
A guarantee that all cases are fatal
lessonCatalog.writing: Compare two community conditions that can change how an outbreak spreads or is managed.

lessonCatalog.title: Explain public health action
lessonCatalog.question: What can a community do that one person cannot do alone?
ideas: Public health uses shared systems such as clean drinking water, waste treatment, disease monitoring and clear guidance to reduce risk for whole populations.
Individual actions can help, but responsibility also sits with public systems. Evaluate a proposed measure by naming its purpose, evidence, feasibility and effects on different groups.
lessonCatalog.model: A water advisory is useful only if people receive clear information and the source of contamination is addressed. Explain both the immediate action and the system repair.
lessonCatalog.check: Which is an example of a community-level prevention system?
options: One person memorizing a symptom list
Changing the name of a disease
lessonCatalog.writing: Evaluate a public health action in the textbook case: what risk is it aimed at, and what evidence would show it helped?

lessonCatalog.title: Map the body’s defences
lessonCatalog.question: How does the body respond when a pathogen crosses a barrier?
ideas: Skin and mucous membranes are physical barriers. If pathogens cross them, inflammation and immune cells help respond. Redness, heat and swelling can be signs of that response.
Antigens are molecules recognized by the immune system. Antibodies can bind specific antigens. A simple pathway from barrier to response helps explain why different defences act at different times.
lessonCatalog.model: A splinter breaks the skin. The damaged barrier allows entry; local inflammation and immune cells respond. The redness is evidence of a response, not proof of which organism is present.
lessonCatalog.check: What is a first-line physical defence?
lessonCatalog.writing: Describe what happens from a broken skin barrier to an immune response, using at least three steps.

lessonCatalog.title: Compare prevention and treatment
lessonCatalog.question: Why does the cause of infection affect the response?
ideas: Vaccination prepares the immune system to respond to a particular pathogen. Active immunity involves the body making its own response; passive immunity involves receiving antibodies made elsewhere.
Antibiotics act against bacteria, not viruses. Treatment choices depend on diagnosis and professional advice; the older textbook is a learning source, not a current treatment guide.
lessonCatalog.model: For a cold caused by a virus, an antibiotic does not target the cause. The reasoning begins with identifying the pathogen type, then choosing a suitable prevention or treatment approach.
lessonCatalog.check: Why is an antibiotic not a treatment for a viral cold?
options: It targets bacteria rather than the virus
It is another name for an antibody
lessonCatalog.writing: Compare a vaccine, an antibody and an antibiotic by what each is intended to do.

lessonCatalog.title: Read genetic information
lessonCatalog.question: How do genes help explain inherited traits?
ideas: DNA carries genetic information. Genes are sections of DNA on chromosomes; inherited versions of a gene can influence traits. Human body cells usually have 23 pairs of chromosomes.
A simple Punnett square models possible allele combinations for a specified trait. It gives probabilities under the stated assumptions, not a guaranteed outcome for an individual child.
lessonCatalog.model: For Tt × Tt with T dominant, the four model combinations are TT, Tt, Tt and tt. Three show the dominant trait in this simple model, while one shows the recessive trait.
lessonCatalog.check: In a simple Tt × Tt cross, what fraction of model outcomes is tt?
lessonCatalog.writing: Draw a Punnett square for Tt × tt. List genotypes and explain one limit of the model.

lessonCatalog.title: Evaluate genetic change and research
lessonCatalog.question: How do we separate evidence from claims about genes?
ideas: A mutation is a change in genetic material. Some mutations have little effect; others can affect function. Mutagens increase the chance of certain changes. A mutation is not automatically inherited.
Genetic research can help identify conditions and support treatment decisions, while raising questions about consent, privacy and fair use. Evaluate a proposal with evidence and the people affected.
lessonCatalog.model: A news story reports a gene linked to a condition. “Linked” does not mean every person with that gene will develop the condition; environment and other genes may also matter.
lessonCatalog.check: Which statement is careful and evidence-based?
options: A genetic change may have different effects depending on context
A Punnett square predicts an individual future with certainty
lessonCatalog.writing: Choose one genetic research use and explain a benefit, a concern and evidence needed before a decision.

glossary.disease: A condition that disrupts normal body function.
glossary.microbe: A microscopic organism or agent; many microbes are harmless or useful.
glossary.bacteria: Single-celled organisms; some species can cause disease.
glossary.virus: An infectious agent that reproduces using host cells.
glossary.communicable: Able to spread between hosts by an infectious route.
glossary.non-communicable: Not spread from person to person by infection.
glossary.sanitation: Practices and systems that maintain healthful conditions and manage waste.
glossary.pasteurization: Controlled heating used to reduce harmful microbes in food or drink.
glossary.sterilization: A process intended to eliminate viable microbes from an item.
glossary.epidemic: An unusual rise in disease cases within a region or population.
glossary.pandemic: An epidemic that spreads across many countries or continents.
glossary.quarantine: Separation or movement restriction after possible exposure to reduce spread.
glossary.migration: Movement of people or other organisms between places.
glossary.public health: Organized work to protect and improve population health.
glossary.advisory: An official notice that communicates a risk and recommended action.
glossary.water treatment: Processes used to make water suitable for its intended use.
glossary.prevention: Action taken to reduce the chance of a problem before it occurs.
glossary.physical defence: A body barrier such as skin or mucous membranes.
glossary.inflammation: A local protective response that can include redness, heat and swelling.
glossary.antigen: A molecule recognized by the immune system.
glossary.antibody: A protein made by immune cells that binds a specific antigen.
glossary.macrophage: An immune cell that engulfs particles and helps coordinate responses.
glossary.vaccine: A preparation that trains an immune response against a particular pathogen.
glossary.active immunity: Protection from an immune response made by a person’s own body.
glossary.passive immunity: Temporary protection from antibodies made elsewhere.
glossary.antibiotic: A medicine that acts against bacteria, not viruses.
glossary.DNA: The molecule that carries much inherited biological information.
glossary.gene: A section of DNA associated with a biological product or trait.
glossary.chromosome: A DNA-containing structure that carries many genes.
glossary.dominant: In a simple allele model, expressed when one copy is present.
glossary.recessive: In a simple allele model, expressed when no dominant copy is present.
glossary.Punnett square: A grid that models possible allele combinations from two parents.
glossary.mutagen: An agent that can increase the chance of genetic changes.
glossary.genetic disorder: A health condition associated with a change in genetic material.
glossary.genetic research: Study of genes and inherited variation to understand biology and health.
